rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the eight-peak elution window and identify critical pairs. The high final organic fraction reduces the risk of missing strongly retained compounds, while a moderate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity.

Keep the gradient fixed and raise temperature to test whether temperature-dependent selectivity separates the central cluster and late doublet. All peaks currently elute well before 10 minutes, leaving ample room for subsequent gradient refinement.

Use a substantially shallower gradient at the better-performing temperature to spread the central cluster and test slope-dependent selectivity. The current short elution window provides room to improve resolution without necessarily exceeding 10 minutes.

The shallower gradient resolved the central cluster but left one near-coeluting pair. Lower temperature by one step to shift selectivity while retaining the improved gradient separation and a likely sub-10-minute last peak.

Flatten the gradient to improve the remaining critical pair at 55 C, while increasing the starting organic fraction to offset the added retention time. This tests whether full resolution can be achieved with the last peak still below 10 minutes.

Reduce the gradient slope another step to improve the sole under-resolved pair, keeping temperature and starting composition fixed. The current last peak at 8.97 minutes leaves about one minute of room before the time penalty begins.

Test a much shallower gradient at 60 C to move beyond the late-pair coelution region while retaining the stronger central-pair selectivity seen at this temperature. A higher starting organic fraction should help keep the last peak near or below 10 minutes.

Lower the starting organic fraction from injection 7 to restore retention and separation in the early cluster. The shallow gradient at 60 C may preserve the improved late-pair separation while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Explore the low-temperature selectivity regime, where the central cluster may separate in a different elution order. The higher starting organic fraction and moderate gradient duration should limit the retention increase while testing an alternative to the near-optimal 55 C methods.
Shorten the fully resolving low-temperature gradient by one step to bring the last peak below 10 minutes. The minimum resolution of 1.98 provides some margin for the steeper gradient.
Injection 10 reached the maximum CRF; retain it as the benchmark. Shorten the gradient one more step to test whether full resolution can be maintained with a faster last peak.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope relative to injection 11 to recover the critical pair’s resolution. This intermediate slope should elute the last peak sooner than injection 10 while potentially retaining its maximum CRF.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to shorten the elution window, while the slightly shallower gradient may help preserve critical-pair resolution. Injection 12 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Reduce the final organic fraction one step to recover the small resolution deficit from injection 13. The last peak should remain comfortably below 10 minutes and may be faster than the current fully resolved benchmark.

Raise the starting organic fraction to shorten retention and reduce the gradient slope to compensate for the critical pair’s loss of resolution. This tests a faster fully resolved method while retaining injection 14 as the benchmark.

Raise temperature one step to test whether the elution window can be shortened without losing full resolution. This isolates temperature selectivity around the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method, injection 15.

Test the fully resolving gradient from injection 14 at 30 C to seek a shorter maximum-CRF run. Relative to injection 16, the lower starting organic fraction and steeper slope may improve the late doublet while preserving separation in the central cluster.

Slightly steepen injection 16’s gradient to test whether the late doublet separates enough to reach full resolution in under eight minutes. The central pair has little resolution margin, so this explicitly probes the trade-off while retaining injection 15 as the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Return to 25 C and test a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to preserve central-pair separation while shortening retention. Injection 15 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Test a gradient slope between injections 13 and 14, targeting just enough central-pair resolution with a shorter elution window. This may improve on injection 15’s 8.99-minute last peak while preserving the maximum CRF.

Test a shallower gradient at 35 C to seek a faster fully resolved separation after the temperature-driven order changes suggested by the 30 C runs. Preserve injection 20 as the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Refine around injection 20 with a slightly shallower slope to increase its narrow resolution margin while keeping the last peak near nine minutes. This targets a maximum-CRF method with more separation margin than injection 20 and a shorter elution window than injection 14.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction at 30 C can shift the central and late critical pairs into simultaneous resolution with a shorter elution window. Injection 20 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Test a modestly steeper slope than injection 15 to locate the fastest fully resolved boundary at this starting composition. Retain injection 20 as the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method if the central pair falls below 1.5.

Use the final injection to strengthen resolution margin around injection 20 by slightly reducing its gradient slope, with the last peak expected to remain below 10 minutes. Injection 20 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method, and the campaign has already achieved the maximum CRF of 1.000.
